---
title: "Exercise 2.6"
---


## Solution

Suppose, for contradiction, that $\mathcal{A}$ is finite. 

Since $X \neq \emptyset$ and $X \in \mathcal{A}$, the assumed property implies that 
$X$ can be written as a disjoint union of two nonempty sets in $\mathcal A$.

Choose one of them and call it $A_1$.
Now apply the same property to $A_1$. Then $A_1$ can be written as a disjoint union of two nonempty sets in $\mathcal A$. 

Choose one of them and call it $A_2$. Since the other piece is also nonempty, we have
$$ A_2 \subsetneq A_1.$$

Repeating this argument, we obtain a strictly decreasing sequence
$$ X \supsetneq A_1 \supsetneq A_2 \supsetneq A_3 \supsetneq \cdots $$
of sets in $\mathcal A$.

This is impossible if $\mathcal A$ is finite. Hence $\mathcal A$ is infinite.

By Exercise 2.8, every infinite $\sigma$-algebra is uncountable. 
Therefore, $\mathcal A$ is uncountable.
